Plot Observed versus Fitted Average Spend

Source: R/GGcov_plot_avg_spend.R
GGcov_plot_avg_spend.Rd

Compares the observed distribution of each customer's average spend per transaction, \(\bar{z}\), with the distribution implied by a fitted gamma-gamma model, as in Figure 3 of Fader and Hardie (2013).

Usage

GGcov_plot_avg_spend(
  fit,
  data,
  max_customers = 5000,
  n = 400,
  xlab = "Average spend per transaction",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Observed versus fitted average spend"
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted model of class "GGcov" from GGcov_MLE.

data

The transaction data frame used to fit the model (subject, spend and covariate columns).

max_customers

Maximum number of customers used to draw the fitted curve. If there are more customers, a random subset is used for the curve (the observed density always uses all customers).

n

Number of points used to draw the curves.

xlab, ylab, main

Axis labels and main title.

Value

Invisibly, a list with the plotted grid, the observed and fitted densities, the number of customers (n_customers) and the number whose covariates vary over time (n_time_varying).

Details

For a customer with \(x\) transactions, the fitted density of \(\bar{z}\) is the average over customers of $$f(\bar{z}) = \frac{1}{c} \, \frac{\Gamma(k + q)}{\Gamma(k)\Gamma(q)} \, \frac{\gamma^q (\bar{z}/c)^{k-1}}{(\gamma + \bar{z}/c)^{k+q}},$$ where \(a_1 = \sum_j e^{w_j\beta'}\), \(a_2 = \sum_j e^{2 w_j\beta'}\), \(k = p a_1^2 / a_2\) and \(c = a_2 / (x a_1)\).

  • If the customer's covariate effect is the same on every transaction (no covariates, or static covariates), then \(k = p x\) and the density is exact.

  • If the covariates change across a customer's transactions, the total spend is a sum of gamma variables with different rates, which has no closed form. The total is then approximated by a gamma distribution with the same mean and variance (given \(\nu_0\)), the Satterthwaite-Welch approximation, which gives the expression above. The plot says so when this approximation is used.

References

Fader, P. S., & Hardie, B. G. S. (2013). The Gamma-Gamma Model of Monetary Value (Research Note No. 025). https://brucehardie.com/notes/025/

Satterthwaite, F. E. (1946). An approximate distribution of estimates of variance components. Biometrics Bulletin, 2(6), 110-114.

Welch, B. L. (1947). The generalization of "Student's" problem when several different population variances are involved. Biometrika, 34(1/2), 28-35.

Moschopoulos, P. G. (1985). The distribution of the sum of independent gamma random variables. Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics, 37, 541-544.
